source: Dasgupta, Lampinen, Chan et al. (2022; PNAS Nexus 2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning
finding: Chinchilla, PaLM 2-M/L, Flan-PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5 judged syllogism validity like humans: they said 'valid' when the conclusion was believable, whatever the logic.
numbers: Syllogism validity task with believable, unbelievable and nonsense-word conditions; humans and 5 models. Significant validity x believability interaction in humans, PaLM 2-L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5 (all p<0.001), none in Chinchilla or PaLM 2-M (they answered mostly by content). Item-level human-model accuracy correlation t(345)=4.98, p<0.001.
quote: humans and models tend to say an argument is valid if the conclusion is belief-consistent, regardless of the actual logical validity
limits: Scoring by option likelihood (DC-PMI correction), not free generation. Figures hold most numbers; text gives tests only.
agent_relevance: Belief bias is a default of the base model, not a rare slip. The agent should never let the model judge validity from content alone.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) same paper, asymmetry section
finding: Same asymmetry as humans: the dominant error is accepting believable invalid conclusions. Rejecting unbelievable valid ones happens but is weaker; most humans and models stay more sensitive to logic when the conclusion is unbelievable.
numbers: Humans and models also lean slightly to 'valid' for nonsense-word syllogisms. GPT-3.5 and large PaLM 2 had high sensitivity to valid arguments but low specificity. Chinchilla and GPT-3.5 answered 'valid' to nearly all nonsense propositions.
limits: Model differences are large; do not assume one model's profile fits another.
agent_relevance: Test the agent on both error directions (accept believable-invalid, reject unbelievable-valid) and on nonsense-content controls, since models differ.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) same paper, humans vs response time
finding: Human accuracy rose with response time. The slowest 15% (over 80 s) were better in the realistic condition but still near chance elsewhere. Wason task replicated with and without a performance bonus.
numbers: Human accuracy vs response time z=4.44, p<0.001. Slow group = top 15% of times, more than 80 s. Bonus vs no-bonus Wason samples: no significant difference.
limits: Observational link between time and accuracy, not a time-pressure manipulation.
agent_relevance: Support for spending more tokens on some items, but time alone did not remove content effects in humans (consistent with G11).

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) same paper, prompt robustness
finding: Content effects survived removing instructions, changing the scoring method, and few-shot examples. Few-shot gave mild accuracy gains and did not remove content effects on syllogisms/Wason. In the natural-language-inference task a few examples took Chinchilla from highly content-biased to near ceiling, and a simple instruction cut bias a lot.
numbers: Instruction-tuned models (Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct) showed no consistent difference in accuracy or content effect against base models. Raw-likelihood scoring with instructions made several models say 'valid' to everything.
quote: a few examples takes Chinchilla from highly content-biased performance to near ceiling performance
limits: The NLI near-ceiling result is for a task where logic is easier to spot; syllogism gains were mild.
agent_relevance: Instructions and few-shot help on easy logic, not on hard syllogisms. Do not rely on a prompt alone to fix belief bias (G7: test at equal tokens).

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models as Soft Reasoners: The Case of Syllogistic Inferences
finding: Twelve open models (Pythia, LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3; 160M to 70B) with zero-shot CoT mostly failed on invalid syllogisms and showed content effects. Instruction tuning raised accuracy on invalid items but lowered it on valid ones.
numbers: Believable set, zero-shot CoT accuracy: LLaMA-3 8B 30.31%, LLaMA-3-inst 8B 50.00%, LLaMA-3 70B 30.63%, LLaMA-3-inst 70B 41.25%. Invalid-syllogism accuracy for base LLaMA-3 8B 0.83%. Human baseline 44.63% valid, 40.97% invalid. Only LLaMA-3-inst 70B showed no content effect (+5.46%).
limits: Open models only, no frontier models. Read from a fetched HTML summary, which noted one internal inconsistency (LLaMA-3 8B content effect -10.44% in Table 1 vs -25.66% in Table 2). 'Nothing follows' task format.
agent_relevance: Small and mid models are poor at saying 'invalid' and 'nothing follows'. A check for invalidity must come from code or a prover, not the model's judgment.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2024) same paper, learning strategies
finding: In-context learning raised accuracy on valid items but did not remove content bias or the invalid-item problem. Supervised fine-tuning was the only method that mostly removed biases without breaking consistency.
numbers: LLaMA-3 8B believable set: ZS-CoT 30.31%, ICL-in 33.39%, SFT 96.25%. Pythia-1.4B: ZS-CoT 14.22%, SFT 92.97%. Bias rate B|U (believable-given-unbelievable) for LLaMA-3 8B: ZS-CoT 22.10%, ICL-out 38.94%, ICL-in 22.94%, SFT 4.28%. Contradictory-answer rate LLaMA-3 8B: ZS-CoT 1.09%, SFT 0.31%.
limits: ICL and SFT run only on Pythia-1.4B and LLaMA-3 8B. SFT is training, which our scaffold excludes; also generalisation to unseen premise counts dropped (Pythia SFT 83.33% at 2 premises to 53.57% at 4).
agent_relevance: Prompt-only fixes (ICL) do not remove the bias in small models. Supports moving the validity decision into code rather than the prompt.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2024) same paper, heuristics
finding: Pretrained model errors fit cognitive-science heuristics. The atmosphere heuristic predicted most of LLaMA-3 8B's mistakes.
numbers: Atmosphere theory predicts 82.97% of invalid-schema mistakes, 62.79% of valid-schema mistakes and 92.31% of correct valid conclusions for LLaMA-3 8B ZS-CoT. Human-model Spearman rho 0.80 (LLaMA-3 70B) and 0.87 (LLaMA-3-inst 70B) on valid believable schemas.
limits: Single model analysed in detail; correlation is not mechanism.
agent_relevance: Errors have predictable shape (form heuristics plus belief), so targeted probes (swap content, keep form) can detect them.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024, NAACL) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: PaLM 2 models beat human accuracy on abstract syllogisms but showed human-like figural (term order) effects and confident fallacies. Models almost never answered 'nothing follows'.
numbers: Human data: Ragni et al. 2019, 139 participants, 64 syllogisms, human accuracy about 50%. Best LM accuracy about 75%; largest model slightly below second-largest. 37 of 64 syllogisms have 'nothing follows' as the only correct answer; LM accuracy on them close to 0% under zero-shot CoT. Llama 2 7B/13B/70B overall similar to humans.
quote: larger LMs behave more like mReasoner instantiations with high SYSTM2 and WEAKEN values
limits: Abstract (no believability manipulation), so it speaks to form biases and not belief bias directly. mReasoner mapping is one of several theories.
agent_relevance: Beliefs are only part of the story: models also have form biases and a strong aversion to 'no valid conclusion'. The agent needs a code check for 'nothing follows'.

source: Eisape et al. (2024) same paper, source of accuracy
finding: The 'trained on human text, so copies human bias' hypothesis got only partial support: bigger models correlate slightly more with human answers, yet beat humans on some syllogisms where humans do worst.
numbers: Scale did not give monotone accuracy gains. For some syllogisms (e.g., EA1: no A are B, all B are C) accuracy fell as model size grew.
quote: We find only partial support for this hypothesis.
limits: Authors speculate code in training data helps; untested.
agent_relevance: Bigger is not always less biased; per-item checks beat trust in scale.

source: Ando et al. (2023) Evaluating LLMs with NeuBAROCO: Syllogistic Reasoning Ability and Human-like Biases
finding: RoBERTa, BART and GPT-3.5 were worst on belief-inconsistent syllogisms of the three content types, in every model.
numbers: NeuBAROCO: 95 symbolic, 167 consistent, 102 inconsistent items, 11 unclear. GPT-3.5 accuracy: symbolic 61.05%, consistent 56.89%, inconsistent 31.37%; overall 51.73%. RoBERTa: consistent 46.11%, symbolic 24.21%, inconsistent 22.55%; overall 34.67%. BART: consistent 45.51%, symbolic 34.74%, inconsistent 15.69%; overall 35.2%. Conversion and atmosphere problems also hard (GPT-3.5 atmosphere 39.42%).
limits: Zero-shot only in this preprint; GPT-3.5 era; 'inconsistent' means any premise or conclusion conflicts with beliefs, mixing premise and conclusion belief.
agent_relevance: A cheap internal test: same logical form, belief-consistent vs belief-inconsistent content, compare accuracy gaps (up to 25 points for GPT-3.5).

source: Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Yanaka et al. (2024) Exploring Reasoning Biases in LLMs Through Syllogism: NeuBAROCO
finding: Extended study in English and Japanese with GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama and others, over 790 NLI items, 80 multiple-choice, 90 translate-and-explain. A Translate-and-Explain CoT prompt separated interpretation errors from reasoning errors.
numbers: Multiple-choice: 13B models 20% (chance) to 30%; 70B and GPT models 42% to 95%; Japanese human overall 53%. Translate-and-Explain: translation accuracy nearly 100%, yet reasoning errors remain. Few-shot exemplars used abstract symbolic problems to stay belief-neutral.
quote: the primary limitations of these models lie in the reasoning process itself, rather than in the interpretation of syllogisms
limits: Accuracy table values read only partly; per-bias numbers (belief gap) not fully captured here.
agent_relevance: Formalising the premises as logic is something models do well (about 100%); the weak step is reasoning over them. Supports 'model translates, code checks'.

source: Valentino, Kim, Ranaldi et al. (2025/2026) Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models Through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
finding: Contrastive activation steering on syllogisms cut content effects and often raised accuracy. In-context learning did not fix content effects and often lowered accuracy. A kNN conditional method (K-CAST) helped models that static steering could not.
numbers: Dataset about 16,000 syllogisms built from WordNet, varying validity and plausibility. Llama 3.2 1B accuracy 58.17% to 73.56%; Acc/CE gain up to 777.27% relative. K-CAST on Llama 3B: up to 15% absolute accuracy gain. Out of distribution: ProntoQA +8.1% (Llama), +5.2% (Qwen); Gemma -16.1% on ProntoQA.
limits: Needs open-weight access. Small models (1B to 9B). Results vary by model; Gemma dropped. Static steering did not help every model.
agent_relevance: Steering is a mechanism-level fix we cannot use with an API model, but it shows belief and validity are separable directions. Prompt-only ICL was no help (G7).

source: Valentino et al. (2025/2026) Steering paper, prior-work claims
finding: Authors state chain-of-thought and fine-tuning boost accuracy but do not fully remove content believability effects, and that biases persist in generated explanations.
numbers: No new numbers; cites Bertolazzi et al. 2024 and Ranaldi, Valentino, Freitas 2025.
quote: biases often persist in the generated explanations
limits: Secondary claim inside an introduction.
agent_relevance: Reasoning text can look sound and still be belief-driven; fits G10 (reasoning text is not evidence).

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi and colleagues (2025) How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility: A Representational Analysis of Content Effects
finding: Validity and plausibility are both linearly encoded in the model and point in similar directions. The more aligned the two directions, the larger the content effect. Steering to pull them apart cut the content effect.
numbers: 10 instruction-tuned models, Qwen-2.5, Qwen-3, Gemma-3, 4B to 32B. 1,280 syllogisms for validity (42% valid), 1,056 conclusions for plausibility. Cosine similarity of validity and plausibility vectors 0.48 to 0.64; controls 0.10 to 0.13 (hypernymy) and -0.12 to -0.17 (harmlessness). Regression: similarity beta=0.557, p=0.017.
quote: both concepts are linearly represented and strongly aligned in representational geometry
limits: Only open models up to 32B; syllogisms only. Read via a fetched summary of the HTML (the last 18,858 characters of the page were read in a second call that returned no usable text).
agent_relevance: Explains why the model cannot separate believable from valid by introspection: the two signals are tangled inside. Separate them outside the model.

source: Same paper (2510.06700), prompting vs steering numbers
finding: Chain-of-thought prompting alone sharply cut the content effect in these instruction-tuned models, and activation steering cut it further without losing accuracy.
numbers: Qwen2.5-32B accuracy zero-shot 81.62%, CoT 94.60%; content effect (CE) 0.348 to 0.096. Qwen3-14B accuracy 86.54% to 96.70%; CE 0.213 to 0.014. Steering at alpha 1.5, zero-shot: Qwen2.5-32B CE 0.348 to 0.072 (accuracy 81.62 to 82.21); Qwen3-14B CE 0.213 to 0.043 (accuracy 86.54 to 96.70).
limits: CE here is a normalized accuracy-gap measure; not comparable to Dasgupta's numbers. Different conclusion from c05/c12: modern instruction-tuned models gain a lot from CoT.
agent_relevance: For recent models, short CoT may already remove most of the bias. Measure first, then decide whether a scaffold step is needed (G7, G11).

source: Valentino et al. (2026) SemEval-2026 Task 11: Disentangling Content and Formal Reasoning in Large Language Models (task overview)
finding: Shared task on content-robust syllogistic validity. Open zero-shot baselines show widespread content effects; newer models shift sharply. Distractor premises hurt; multilingual settings increase susceptibility to content bias. Explicit symbolic verification was the most reliable strategy.
numbers: Four subtasks (English/multilingual, standard/noisy premises). Metric: content effect = mean of valid-vs-invalid and plausible-vs-implausible accuracy gaps; combined score CS = Acc / (1 + ln(1+CE)). Abstract gives no per-team numbers.
limits: Only the abstract page was available; no leaderboard values read.
agent_relevance: A public benchmark with a built-in content-effect metric; we can reuse it to test our agent's belief-bias handling, and its main lesson is 'verify symbolically'.

source: Kartac, Onderkova, Bronec, Kasner, Lango, Dusek (2026) UFAL-CUNI at SemEval-2026 Task 11: Modular Neuro-symbolic Method for Syllogistic Reasoning
finding: A 4B reasoning LLM translates each sentence to first-order logic and a prover (Prover9) decides validity. This cut content effect strongly against asking the same LLM to judge validity directly.
numbers: Test accuracy: subtask 1 95.29 (CS 39.08, rank 19 of 35); subtask 2 97.37 (rank 6 of 14); subtask 3 93.75 (rank 8 of 13); subtask 4 84.90, CE 1.37, CS 45.20 (rank 4 of 15). Ablations: direct zero-shot classification about 10 points lower accuracy with sharply higher CE; LLM as prover more than 15 points lower; direct Prover9 syntax 18% of formulas had syntax errors and over 10 points lower accuracy.
limits: Pipeline errors propagate; Aristotelian syllogisms only. Qwen3 4B beat the 30B-A3B MoE in accuracy, so size is not the driver.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for our design: the model parses, code decides. Translate sentences one at a time with a running symbol map to limit content leakage.

source: UFAL-CUNI paper (2605.04941), metric analysis
finding: The official combined score over-amplifies random noise: an unbiased model with high accuracy still has a nonzero expected measured content effect, so near-perfect systems are penalised for single errors.
numbers: Only four submissions showed content effect above the 95th percentile of simulated unbiased models (subtask 1). Expected CE about 2.3 for a 98%-accurate unbiased model.
limits: Applies to this task's group sizes (N per group), derived with a Gaussian approximation that the authors say is weak near 100% accuracy.
agent_relevance: When we measure belief bias in our agent, test the gap against a null with the same accuracy; small gaps are noise.

source: Kim, Valentino, Freitas (2025, Findings of ACL) Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
finding: A small circuit of attention heads handles syllogistic schemes in models above 60% accuracy. Belief bias is only partly separable: extra heads encoding commonsense knowledge contaminate the circuit.
numbers: Circuit necessary and sufficient for schemes where models exceed 60% accuracy. No other numbers on the abstract page.
quote: partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that belief and logic are mixed at the mechanism level, so a clean separation must happen outside the network.

source: Ranaldi, Valentino, Freitas (2025) Improving Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Quasi-Symbolic Abstractions (QuaSAR)
finding: A prompt-level scaffold: the model abstracts only the relevant variables and predicates into a quasi-symbolic form before reasoning. Aims to disentangle content from logic.
numbers: Accuracy up to 8% over CoT methods; better robustness and consistency on adversarial MMLU-Redux and GSM-Symbolic.
quote: CoT explanations are susceptible to content biases that negatively affect their robustness and faithfulness
limits: Abstract only; no belief-bias-specific test; the gain is on general benchmarks.
agent_relevance: A cheap prompt-only operator to try: abstract content to symbols, reason, then map back. Needs an equal-token test against plain CoT (G7).

source: Seals and Shalin (2024, NAACL) Evaluating the Deductive Competence of Large Language Models
finding: On the Wason selection task, LLMs did poorly in the standard form. Changing format and content shifted results but did not raise overall performance, and the pattern differed from humans.
numbers: No figures on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Wason task, not syllogisms.
agent_relevance: Realistic framing does not rescue the model the way it helps humans; do not expect content tricks to substitute for a check.

source: Olausson, Gu, Lipkin et al. (2023, EMNLP) LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
finding: The LLM only translates to first-order logic and a prover does the inference. Failures of this method and of CoT differ and complement each other.
numbers: ProofWriter: StarCoder+ 15.5B with LINC beats GPT-3.5 CoT by 38 points and GPT-4 CoT by 10 points. GPT-4 with LINC 26 points above its CoT on ProofWriter; comparable on FOLIO.
limits: Abstract only. Not a belief-bias study. Translation errors, not reasoning errors, dominate failures.
agent_relevance: Older and general version of the neuro-symbolic split. Because errors differ from CoT, using both and flagging disagreement fits G1 (doubt on a signal).

source: FregeLogic at SemEval-2026 Task 11: hybrid neurosymbolic architecture for content-robust syllogistic validity prediction
finding: Ensemble of several LLMs, with disputed cases deferred to the Z3 solver.
numbers: Self-reported by a participant: 94.3% accuracy, content effect 2.85, combined score 41.88 in nested 5-fold cross-validation, N=960.
limits: Seen only as a search-result snippet; not opened. Not an official leaderboard result.
agent_relevance: Pattern: models vote, disagreement triggers an external solver. Matches G1 and G4.

source: Proofbusters / pamaldi systems at SemEval-2026 Task 11 (as reported in search summary)
finding: Several teams had the LLM extract the mood and figure of each syllogism, then checked the form against the 24 valid Aristotelian forms in code.
numbers: None captured.
limits: Second-hand from a search summary; system papers not opened.
agent_relevance: The cheapest code check for categorical syllogisms: a lookup table of 24 valid forms after content is stripped.

source: Evans, Barston, Pollard (1983) as restated in Dasgupta et al. (2022)
finding: The human baseline the LLM papers compare against: people accepted believable invalid conclusions about 90% of the time; rejection of unbelievable valid ones was weaker.
numbers: 90% acceptance of believable invalid syllogisms (as quoted by Dasgupta et al.).
quote: Participants were very likely (90% of the time) to mistakenly say an invalid syllogism was valid if the conclusion was believable
limits: Second-hand figure; not checked against the 1983 paper. Later work (not opened here) reanalysed the effect with signal detection.
agent_relevance: Gives the reference size for LLM comparisons; check the original before quoting it.

source: Ozeki et al. (2024) NeuBAROCO, related work section on Dasgupta and Eisape
finding: Positions earlier LLM studies: Dasgupta et al. used binary valid/invalid judgments by conclusion believability; Eisape et al. used abstract syllogisms. NeuBAROCO adds Japanese and the Translate-and-Explain analysis, extending Ando et al.'s 375-item GPT-3.5 preliminary to 790 items.
numbers: 375 items (Ando 2023, GPT-3.5 zero-shot only) vs 790 NLI items here.
limits: Citation map only.
agent_relevance: Where to look next for citations: Dasgupta 2022, Eisape 2023, Bertolazzi 2024, Ando 2023.

source: Valentino et al. steering paper, ICL result
finding: Few-shot examples in the prompt are not enough to cut content effects and in most cases lowered accuracy; the best syllogism results came from steered models.
numbers: Table 1 compares zero-shot and ICL settings across Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2 9B; exact ICL numbers not captured.
quote: ICL via few-shot examples is not sufficient to mitigate content effect biases and, in most cases, can have the detrimental effect of reducing accuracy
limits: Small open models; fixed few-shot examples.
agent_relevance: Few-shot demos are not a safe fix. Treat any prompt addition as a hypothesis to test at equal tokens.
